Network of 1,653 X profiles reportedly pushed Israelis to back Likud in coordinated Hebrew posts, then went back to promoting the shah’s son
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks following exit polls in Jerusalem on 28 October (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)
Off
A network of 1,653 X accounts posing as Iranian users amplified Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s election campaign ahead of last week’s vote, Haaretz reported on Friday.
The accounts posted messages in Hebrew urging Israelis to vote for Netanyahu “on behalf of the Iranian people”.
The accounts, which claimed to belong to Iranians living in Iran or abroad, appeared to coordinate their activity. Their operators remain unidentified.
Activity intensified on election day, when multiple accounts published identical messages and responded to posts in coordinated bursts.
Two accounts, for example, shared 109 identical posts, compared with just four expected through organic activity, according to Haaretz’s analysis.
They also responded simultaneously, or within five minutes of each other, to 232 posts by 53 different accounts.
On election morning, two accounts posted the same Hebrew message about an hour apart: “We call on you to support Benjamin Netanyahu to finish the job”, accompanied by the hashtag #IsraeliElections2026.
“Tomorrow, vote only for the Likud party,” one account wrote in response to a Netanyahu post at 10pm on the eve of the election.
“Vote for Benjamin Netanyahu,” another posted twice within two minutes after midnight.
“Dear people of Israel, if you want to be protected from the Islamic Republic and the Axis of Resistance, vote,” read another message, published in Hebrew and English at around 2am.

Inside Centcom podcast with Admiral Brad Cooper (left) and Fleet Master Chief Lateef Compton (Screengrab/Centcom/YouTube)
Off
The Pentagon has entered its podcast bro era, and viewers have widely derided its debut.
As the cost of the US-Israeli war on Iran spirals for American taxpayers, US Central Command (Centcom) launched its official podcast on Thursday.
The first episode of Inside Centcom pairs Admiral Brad Cooper, who leads the US command overseeing the war, with Fleet Master Chief Lateef Compton.
In the 12-minute episode on YouTube, Cooper jokes about stealing French fries from Compton’s lunch. The pair touch only briefly on the deeply unpopular war, now in its ninth month. Centcom turned off comments on YouTube.
The podcast looks like an attempt to reach young men who might one day fight Washington’s wars in the Middle East.
"It's called service for a reason. You're going to give more than you're going to get. But if you find satisfaction in giving, you'll have no greater satisfaction than serving in the United States military in particular," claimed Cooper.
"It’s been a busy year," Compton joked at the start of the episode, a passing nod to a war that has killed thousands in Iran and left the US mired in another Middle East conflict.
Cooper said nothing about the US strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school in Minab, southern Iran, on 28 February, the first day of the war.

Prominent British YouTuber Mohammed Hijab has claimed that counter-terrorism police tried to recruit him as an informant after seizing his devices.
Hijab, whose legal name is Mohamed Hegab, describes himself as a philosopher of religion pursuing a PhD in the subject at the University of Birmingham.
He has more than a million subscribers on YouTube and frequently takes parts in debates on religion, as well as political issues.
In a post on X on Wednesday, Hijab said: "I want this on the record.
"In May, counter terrorism police stopped me without explanation, seized my devices and read more than ten thousand messages. My phone came back on 11 September. No further questions."
Hijab added: "Their notes, disclosed through my subject access request. One line reads 'Doesn’t want to be an informant.'"
He posted a screenshot of a page marked "REDACTED EXCERPT - Unrelated content removed" which has the Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) logo on it and the heading: "Examining Officer's Notes - Continued".
All the notes in the screenshot are redacted apart from a handwritten line which says: "Doesnt want to be an informant."
It is unclear whether the entire document was redacted by the police, or whether Hijab blacked it out himself to protect sensitive information.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Gaza records more birth defects in nine months than in all of 2022, Wafa reports
data.author: Mee User
data.summary:
Gaza records more birth defects in nine months than in all of 2022, Wafa reports
The number of birth defects recorded among newborns in Gaza during the first nine months of 2026 has exceeded the total reported for the whole of 2022, the year before Israel’s war on the territory began, the Palestinian news agency Wafa has reported.
A medical source in Gaza told Wafa that 260 cases were recorded between January and September, compared with 184 cases in all of 2022.
The source said 322 cases were recorded in 2025, a 75 percent increase on the 2022 figure.
Possible contributing factors include maternal malnutrition, exposure to environmental pollutants and disruptions to prenatal care during the war, the source said, calling for an independent international scientific investigation.
The source cautioned that the figures alone do not establish the rate of congenital anomalies among newborns or determine their causes.
A January 2025 report by Human Rights Watch said pregnant women in Gaza faced serious health risks because of the war, the blockade, damage to health facilities and shortages of food, water and medicine.

data.title: Middle East Eye: A deadly raid tests a revolutionary town’s faith in Syria's new government
data.author: Natacha Danon
data.summary:
A deadly raid tests a revolutionary town’s faith in Syria's new government
Submitted by
Natacha Danon
on
Fri, 11/06/2026 - 10:04
Five people were killed in the town of Rankous after a government raid on alleged Islamic State sympathisers
A blue mosque rebuilt by residents stands atop a hill in the small town of Rankous (MEE/Ammar Stifi)
Off
Driving north from Damascus, I made my way toward the Lebanese border, through barren apple and cherry orchards, up into the Qalamoun mountains.
As the town of Rankous came into view, 33-year old Abu Jad, a former member of the Free Syrian Army (FSA) who fought against former ruler Bashar al-Assad, was waiting for me on the main street. He waved at me from the darkened window of his SUV and greeted me with a grim smile.
“Welcome to Rankous, the capital of the revolution in Qalamoun,” he said.
Early in the morning of 22 October, the town’s habitual calm was shattered when Syrian security forces stormed homes and shops, rounding up 45 people and killing five.
According to the Ministry of Interior, the victims had links to the Islamic State (IS), held “extremist ideas,” and had “declared the Syrian state as infidel”.
Three of the victims were unarmed at the time, while two opened fire on the security forces, killing two of its members, according to residents.
For three consecutive days, hundreds of residents and visitors converged on the town square, where a collective wedding was supposed to be held in less than two weeks’ time.
Instead of celebrating life, they were left mourning their sons who had lost their childhood to the war, only to be killed after it finally came to an end.
For the people of Rankous, the latest bloodshed has deepened a sense of loss and injustice in a town that gave hundreds of lives to the revolution. Many feel that their community has been left on the margins of the post-Assad order, with little representation in state institutions or support to rebuild.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Houthis and Yemeni government blame each other for Taiz market attack that killed 30
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Houthis and Yemeni government blame each other for Taiz market attack that killed 30
Yemen’s Houthis and the internationally recognised government have blamed each other for a deadly attack on a market in Taiz province earlier on Friday.
The Houthis said Saudi aircraft carried out the strikes, while the government accused the group of firing a ballistic missile at the market and called the attack a “war crime”.
“Saudi enemy aircraft targeted the market in Al-Waziya city with several strikes,” Houthi health ministry spokesman Anis al-Asbahi said, according to the Houthi-run Saba news agency.
The group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the aircraft had taken off from Saudi Arabia’s Khamis Mushait base.
Meanwhile, local authorities in Taiz blamed “indiscriminate Houthi missile fire” and denied any air strikes had taken place.
The Houthi health ministry put the toll at 30 dead and eight wounded, and said rescue teams were still searching for bodies under the rubble at the market, which lies in a Houthi-held area of the province.
Government forces said on Friday that they had recaptured several areas of Taiz from the Houthis. The province lies near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key oil shipping route.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Syria sends military advisers to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks, sources say
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Syria sends military advisers to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks, sources say
Syria has sent a small number of military personnel to Saudi Arabia to advise and train forces as the kingdom comes under attack from Yemen’s Houthis, Reuters reported, citing two Syrian military sources and a senior US official.
The US official said Syrian advisers and training teams were travelling to Saudi Arabia to improve the combat effectiveness of Saudi and Yemeni units based there. The two Syrian military sources, who had direct knowledge of the matter, said scores of personnel had travelled to Saudi Arabia in recent weeks.
A senior Syrian diplomat told Reuters that "any suggestion of military deployments at this stage is premature" and that Syria remained focused on internal security, border protection and reconstruction.
The diplomat added that a defence cooperation agreement the two countries signed on Wednesday "specifically includes advisory support, training and exchange of expertise".
The two countries signed the agreement in Riyadh during a visit by Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for the second time in less than a month. The full terms of the deal were not made public.
Turkey, a close ally of Damascus, recently ratified a defence pact signed in Mecca in August by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani told a recent conference in Bahrain that talks were under way on Syria joining the pact.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Rights groups condemn Bahrain's largest mass trial of Shia clerics in history
data.author: Alex MacDonald
data.summary:
Rights groups condemn Bahrain's largest mass trial of Shia clerics in history
Submitted by
Alex MacDonald
on
Fri, 11/06/2026 - 14:50
Sixty clerics face prison after interrogations that campaigners say involved torture and forced confessions
Visitors take photos of the Matam Bin Rajab mosque in Manama, Bahrain, 6 November 2026 (Hamad Mohammed/Reuters)
Off
Bahrain is set to hold the largest mass trial of Shia clerics in the country's history, with rights groups accusing the judiciary of obtaining confessions through coercion and torture.
On Sunday, a Bahraini court is set to hand down judgments to 69 defendants, among them 60 clerics, on charges of membership of a terrorist group, attempting to overthrow the "constitutional regime" and trying to promote Iran's political ideology.
According to testimony obtained by the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (Bird), the defendents were subjected to a range of abuses, including forced standing, prolonged blindfolding and handcuffing, sleep deprivation, and threats of physical and sexual violence against them and their families.
They were also threatened with revocation of their citizenship and deportation.
Sheikh Mohammed Saeed Al-Taitoon, a 62-year-old cleric, told investigators he was blindfolded and restrained for a week, and forced to stand despite severe urinary bleeding and kidney stones, while being denied necessary surgery.
Another, 57-year-old Sayed Moosa Jawad Alwedaie, told investigators he had been beaten, tortured with electricity and left naked.
Twenty rights organisations, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, called on the authorities to release those arbitrarily detained and drop charges based on peaceful religious activities, and to investigate allegations of mistreatment and torture.

data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Seafarer killed in Gulf as Iran says ships ablaze in Hormuz
A seafarer was killed when a Greek-owned oil tanker was struck by a projectile in the Gulf, its owner said on Friday, as Iran said several tankers had caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Marshall Islands-flagged Velos Sapphire was sailing empty to Bahrain when it was hit on Thursday, Athens-based Velos Tankers said in a statement carried by the Greek news agency ANA.
The company said an unidentified projectile likely caused the explosion after striking the vessel’s port quarter and starting a fire.
Iranian media reported on Thursday that five oil tankers and a tugboat had caught fire after hitting mines in the strait.
On Friday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two more “violating” tankers had struck mines and were on fire, one east of the strait and the other inside it.
“The two tankers had deactivated all of their navigation and identification systems and were attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz… with the support of the aggressor and terrorist American military,” the IRGC said in a statement.

House Democratic leaders, including minority leader Hakeem Jeffries (second left) and Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee chair Suzan DelBene, hold a press conference in Washington on 4 November 2026 after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress (Tom Brenner/Getty Images via AFP)

The political tsunami that swept across the US on 3 November was extraordinary in both its scale and implications. The electoral flood that overwhelmed the Republicans was not simply another midterm correction.
It was a sweeping rejection of Donald Trump's presidency: his economic policies, his wars, the corruption charges against his administration and his increasingly confrontational use of presidential power.
But the more consequential question is what happens next. Will this upheaval produce a fundamental reassessment of American foreign policy, particularly towards Israel, Palestine, Iran, and the wider Middle East? Or will the Democratic establishment try to restore the familiar bipartisan consensus that helped produce the very crises now confronting Washington? The answer will shape American politics throughout 2027 and beyond.
The scale of the Republican defeat exceeded expectations. Democrats captured both chambers of Congress. They flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa, North Carolina, Ohio and Maine, bringing their total to at least 54. The count in Alaska favours the Democrats, and Mississippi could still elect its first Democratic senator since 1982.

data.title: Middle East Eye: US issues new Iran sanctions as Trump says talks with Tehran going 'very well'
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
US issues new Iran sanctions as Trump says talks with Tehran going 'very well'
US President Donald Trump said on Friday that his administration was in talks with Iranian representatives, telling reporters: "We are doing very well with Iran."
His comments came as the US Treasury Department imposed new Iran-related sanctions on eight entities based in Canada, according to a notice on its website.
In a separate move on Friday, the Treasury blocked US banks from dealing with MEXC Global, a cryptocurrency exchange registered in the Seychelles.
It accused the exchange of handling at least $16bn in illegal transactions linked to Iran, North Korea and Russia, helping them get around sanctions.
On Thursday, the Treasury sanctioned companies and individuals in India and Turkey that it accused of helping Iran evade restrictions on its oil exports and airlines.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the same day that Washington would continue to pursue anyone supporting Tehran.
